column1: # English words that are cousins of the French ones Weft teaches.
# The French pack shipped with no etymon and no note on any of its 587
# entries, while Old English had 544 and 126. Two of the things that make
# Weft worth using — the discoveries feed, and the "you already know this"
# line in the tooltip — are built from exactly those two fields. So for a
# French learner, the single most mass-market language in the product, both
# features were simply blank, and the marketing had to lead with Old English
# because Old English was the only place they worked.
# The French version of that story is better, not worse: a very large part
# of English vocabulary arrived from French, and most of the rest shares a
# Latin root with it. "You know more French than you think" is a truer and
# more encouraging thing to tell a beginner than anything Old English can
# Two relationships, kept apart on purpose
# DESCENT (the etymon column) is used only where English genuinely took the
# word from French or Old French. "English forest comes from forêt" is a
# claim about borrowing and it has to be true.
# A descent is a claim about the English word, so that is where it is
# checked. Twelve of the thirty this file first held were false, and all in
# one way: each paired an English word with its French translation and
# called the translation its source. "English money comes from argent" —
# money is Old French monoie. "answer" is Old English and "gift" Old Norse;
# "rich" is Old English rīce, which French riche only reshaped. Words that
# mean the same thing are not, for that reason, related.
# COUSIN (the note column) is used where French and English share a root —
# almost always Latin — and the English relative is a different, usually
# more formal word. cheval did not become an English word; it shares a root
# with cavalry. Writing that as a descent would be wrong, and the discoveries
# feed would then state it as fact.
# A note says "the root of English X" only where English took X from this
# very word: petit gave petty, and pays gave peasant. Where both come down
# from Latin it says "shares a root with". That is the descent/cousin line
# again, one column over, and nine notes once had it backwards — "cheval,
# the root of cavalry", when cavalry came through Italian from caballus.
# Nothing here is a guess, and every line says where it was checked: see
# Sources below. Where the relationship was arguable — famille and family
# both descend from Latin familia but English took it from the Latin
# directly — it was left out rather than fudged. A charming etymology that
# turns out to be false costs more trust than a blank field.
# A note must never quote the French word back at the reader. Three did:
# "route — shares a root with English “route”" is circular and says
# nothing. tools/verify-packs.mjs fails on it now.
# For descent, value is the English word. For cousin, it is the note text.
# The dictionary entries a claim was checked against, separated by spaces:
# A claim has to cite the etymonline entry for every English word it names
# — a descent's word, or every word its note quotes — and the Wiktionary
# entry for its French word, on every row its lemma has. `npm run cousins`
# refuses a claim that does not, with or without --force. Twenty-nine of the
# 116 claims this file once held were false, every one about a word nobody
# had looked up, and looking up both words is the whole of the check they
# All 115 lines were checked against the entries they cite on 2026-10-01.
# English borrowed these from French or Old French.
# Words spelled identically in both languages are deliberately absent.
# The pack builder skips a translation that maps to itself, so the
# reader never meets them woven, and a discoveries line reading
# "fruit is simply fruit" is filler about a word that was never shown.
# A shared root, usually Latin; the English relative is usually the formal
# word. "the root of" where English took the word from this one.
